Macroscopic fat (areas < -10/-20 HU) in a renal mass is almost diagnostic of angiomyolipoma. However, about 5% of angiomyolipomas are "lipid-poor": on CT they appear as homogeneous solid masses, often hyperdense on unenhanced images, with homogeneous and prolonged enhancement, and they cannot be reliably distinguished from a carcinoma (especially papillary or chromophobe).
For this reason a solid renal mass without visible fat must be managed as potentially malignant: chemical-shift MRI and biopsy may help, but the diagnosis often comes only with surgery.
In this patient, histology after nephrectomy showed an angiomyolipoma.
